value.question: Explain what a hash table is and why lookups are usually described as O(1).

steps.description: Search for technical explanations of hash table data structure, hash functions, and how lookups work
Research the amortized/average-case O(1) time complexity analysis of hash table lookups, including collision handling

key_findings: A hash table is a data structure used to insert, look up, and remove key-value pairs quickly, operating on a hashing concept where each key is translated by a hash function into a distinct index in an array (geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/hash-table-data-structure).

Hash table lookup is O(1) because it is an array with a map to the index: an array lookup is O(1) since memory is addressable (address(i) = base + i * element_size), and a hash table adds one constant-time step (computing an integer index via a hash function) before the array access (spacecomplexity.ai/blog/hash-table-time-complexity).

The average-case time complexity for lookup, insertion, and deletion is O(1), but worst case may require O(n) time where n is the number of elements in the table (geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/hash-table-data-structure).

Collisions are resolved through techniques such as chaining, open addressing, and double hashing; a decent hash function with even distribution and proper load factor management reduces collisions and ensures quick lookup speeds (geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/hash-table-data-structure).
gaps: The evidence does not fully detail how specific collision resolution techniques (e.g., chaining, open addressing, double hashing) affect the amortized O(1) claim under varying load factors, beyond stating that average-case is O(1).

The evidence does not specify the conditions under which O(1) degrades to O(n) in concrete scenarios beyond noting worst-case behavior with collisions.

value.text: A hash table is a data structure used to insert, look up, and remove key-value pairs quickly, operating on the hashing concept where each key is translated by a hash function into an index in an array. Lookups are described as O(1) because a hash table is effectively an array with a map to the index: an array lookup is O(1) since memory is addressable, and the hash table adds the constant-time step of computing a bucket index before the array access. However, this is the average-case time complexity; worst case may require O(n) time where n is the number of elements in the table, typically when collisions occur. Maintaining O(1) depends on a good hash function, collision resolution techniques like chaining, open addressing, and double hashing, and dynamic resizing to keep an ideal load factor.
